sections.title: Lesson 01: Sequence models and transformer workload

keyTerms.definition: Unit 01 of CS229S, covering sequence models and transformer workload.
The evidence label on every lesson claim, here PLANNED with source attribution pending.

recall.question: What unit and concepts does this lesson cover?
recall.answer: Unit cs229s-U01, concepts C01 to C12, calendar-anchored to Week 1, Sep 27, Transformer Architecture.

keyTerms.definition: The fixed structure every concept carries, from source and scope to visual units.
The shared symbol reference that every lesson follows.

recall.question: What does each concept in the lesson carry?
recall.answer: The 15-item contract: source and scope, motivating question and toy, mental model, objects and shapes, derivation, computed example, implementation and checks, costs, nearest alternative, failure case, research reading, exercises, and visual units.

keyTerms.definition: The RNN's forced order: step t needs the state from step t minus 1.
The longest chain of sequential dependencies from input to output.
The T by T matrix that lets every token read every other token directly.
The per-layer work of attention, all of it parallel.

recall.question: Why did the field move from RNNs to attention for long sequences?
recall.answer: RNNs force T sequential steps with a longest path of T minus 1 handoffs. Attention connects any two tokens in one hop and runs all pairs in parallel.

recall.question: What is the cost tradeoff of attention versus RNN?
recall.answer: Attention needs O(T^2 d) work and O(T^2) memory per layer. The RNN needs O(T) work and constant memory. The trade is parallelism for memory.

recall.question: When does attention fail where an RNN still runs?
recall.answer: At very long T the T^2 score matrix exceeds device memory. Example: T = 100000, n = 64 needs 100000^2 times 2 bytes.

keyTerms.definition: Learning from raw text by predicting each next token, at large scale.
The pretraining objective: every position's next token is a free label.
Exp of mean negative log-likelihood; the training-health metric.
Fine-tuning erasing pretraining knowledge through too large a rate or too many steps.

recall.question: Why does pretraining work with no human labels?
recall.answer: Every position's next token is a free label, so D tokens give D training examples. The gradient pushes probability toward observed continuations.

recall.question: What is the main risk of fine-tuning, and the fix?
recall.answer: Catastrophic forgetting: task loss falls while general perplexity rises. Fix with a smaller learning rate and early stopping on a held-out set.

recall.question: How do pretraining and fine-tuning costs compare?
recall.answer: Pretraining dominates at 6PD FLOPs. Fine-tuning is often under 1 percent of pretraining but decides task behavior.

keyTerms.definition: One of h parallel attention units, each working in a d-sized subspace.
The (B, h, T, T) matrix of query-key compatibilities before softmax.
The function that turns scores into weights that sum to one over keys.

recall.question: From n = 8, h = 2, T = 4, what are the shapes of Q and the scores?
recall.answer: Q is (1, 2, 4, 4) and scores A are (1, 2, 4, 4), with d = n / h = 4.

recall.question: Why must n be divisible by h?
recall.answer: Otherwise the head split is undefined and code must raise.

recall.question: What does softmax run over in attention?
recall.answer: The last axis, the keys. Each row of A sums to 1.

keyTerms.definition: Floating-point operations; the currency of training cost.
Training costs 6P FLOPs per token: 2P forward plus 4P backward.
Limited by arithmetic throughput rather than memory traffic.
Storing a subset of activations and recomputing the rest to save memory.

recall.question: Where does the 3x training-versus-inference factor come from?
recall.answer: Forward is 2P FLOPs per token. Backward is 4P: 2P for activation gradients plus 2P for weight gradients. Total 6P.

recall.question: Why does the backward pass need the activations?
recall.answer: The backward walk assigns blame at each station and needs the ingredients that were present, so training stores every layer's activations.

recall.question: When does the backward-to-forward ratio exceed 2x?
recall.answer: With activation checkpointing the backward pass recomputes the forward, pushing the ratio toward 3x.

keyTerms.definition: Parameters per transformer layer with d_ff = 4n: 4n^2 attention plus 8n^2 MLP.
The V by n table that maps token IDs to vectors.
Reusing one V by n matrix for the input embedding and output head.
An MLP variant with three matrices that breaks the 12n^2 constant.

recall.question: How do you get 12n^2 parameters per layer?
recall.answer: Attention has four n by n matrices (4n^2). The MLP has (n, 4n) and (4n, n) (8n^2). Total 12n^2, plus V n embeddings.

recall.question: Where does the 7B-class number come from?
recall.answer: n = 4096, L = 32, V = 32000: 32 times 12 times 4096^2 is about 6.44B, plus 131M embeddings, about 6.57B total.

recall.question: When does the 12n^2 formula break?
recall.answer: SwiGLU MLPs use three matrices, MoE layers multiply by expert count, and tied embeddings halve the embedding term.

keyTerms.definition: Memory for intermediate tensors, which training must keep for backward.
The per-layer (B, T, n) tensor whose storage costs 2BTnL bytes in fp16.
Stored keys and values that keep inference memory at O(T) per layer.
Adam's fp32 m and v plus the master weights, about 8 bytes per parameter.

recall.question: Write the residual-stream byte formula.
recall.answer: 2 times B times T times n times L bytes in fp16, for the residual stream alone.

recall.question: Why does training OOM when the model weights fit?
recall.answer: Activations: at B = 8, T = 2048, n = 4096, L = 32, the residual stream alone is 4 GiB and the MLP intermediate is 16 GiB. The belt, not the factory, causes most OOMs.

recall.question: Why does fp16 not halve all memory?
recall.answer: Master weights, optimizer states, and some activations stay in fp32. A 7B model needs 14 GB for fp16 weights but over 80 GB with Adam states.

keyTerms.definition: Stored keys and values, shape (B, h, t, d) per layer after t steps.
The rule that each position sees only past positions.
Limited by bytes moved, not FLOPs; the decode regime at batch 1.

recall.question: In one decode step, what is recomputed and what is reused?
recall.answer: One new key and value are computed; all t cached pairs are read. Nothing is recomputed from scratch.

recall.question: Why is decode memory-bandwidth bound at batch 1?
recall.answer: Each weight is used once per token, so arithmetic intensity is low, and each step reads O(T) KV traffic per layer.

recall.question: When does the KV cache itself become the bottleneck?
recall.answer: At huge batch: batch 256 at T = 8192 needs about 1.1 TB of cache, which caps the batch.

keyTerms.definition: FLOPs per byte moved; it decides whether a regime is compute- or bandwidth-bound.
The batch size past which extra batch adds little statistical value per FLOP.

recall.question: Name the five training-versus-inference contrasts.
recall.answer: Parallelism: B times T vs B. FLOPs per token: 6P vs 2P. Bound by: compute vs memory bandwidth. Memory: activations O(BTL) vs KV cache. Objective: minimize loss vs minimize latency.

recall.question: What is the decode time floor for 7B fp16 at 2 TB/s?
recall.answer: 14 GB of weight traffic per token over 2000 GB/s gives 0.007 s, about 143 tokens/s max.

recall.question: What goes wrong past the critical batch size?
recall.answer: Doubling B doubles cost per step with flat loss progress. Measure gradient noise scale first.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence length where attention cost overtakes MLP cost.
The per-token feedforward block costing 16n^2 FLOPs with d_ff = 4n.
The crossover point: 4Tn equals 24n^2 when T equals 6n.

recall.question: Derive the T = 6n crossover.
recall.answer: MLP is 16n^2, projections 8n^2, scores 4Tn per token per layer. Set 4Tn = 24n^2 to get T = 6n.

recall.question: At n = 4096 and T = 2048, which part dominates, and by how much?
recall.answer: MLP: 16 times 4096^2 = 2.68e8. Scores: 4 times 2048 times 4096 = 3.36e7. The MLP dominates 8 to 1.

recall.question: Why is the claim 'attention is always the bottleneck' wrong?
recall.answer: At T = 2048, n = 4096 the MLP is 8x the attention scores. A profiler that only optimizes attention leaves 89 percent of FLOPs untouched.

keyTerms.definition: How FLOPs, memory, and KV cache grow with sequence length T.
The quadratic term: attention scores cost 4T^2n FLOPs and 2BhT^2 bytes naive.
Tiled attention that removes the T^2 memory term.

recall.question: When T doubles, what doubles and what quadruples?
recall.answer: Scores FLOPs and memory quadruple (T^2). MLP FLOPs and the KV cache double (linear in T).

recall.question: Which scaling wall is hard and which is soft?
recall.answer: T^2 memory is the hard wall. T^2 FLOPs is a soft wall because compute can be bought.

recall.question: How does max batch scale with T in the cache-bound regime?
recall.answer: Max batch falls as 1/T. Fit the curve and report the constant.

keyTerms.definition: Exp of mean negative log-likelihood; the training-health metric.
Accuracy on a fixed task set; the sparring session for capability claims.
Test text appearing in training, which makes loss look great and mean nothing.

recall.question: Define perplexity in one sentence.
recall.answer: Perplexity is exp of mean negative log-likelihood; mean NLL of 2.5 nats gives perplexity 12.2.

recall.question: Why must you never promote on perplexity alone?
recall.answer: Lower loss does not guarantee task wins: the toy model B has higher loss yet wins the quiz 4/4 versus 3/4. Use perplexity for training health, task accuracy for capability, human eval for deployment.

recall.question: What is eval contamination?
recall.answer: Test text appearing in training. Loss looks great and means nothing; check for it before celebrating.

keyTerms.definition: The reference method run under identical conditions: data, budget, metric.
Your method minus one part, to isolate what matters.
Time of baseline over time of method at equal quality.

recall.question: Define baseline and ablation in one line each.
recall.answer: Baseline: the reference method under identical conditions. Ablation: your method minus one part.

recall.question: How did a 2x speedup become a 0.6x slowdown?
recall.answer: Against naive attention the variant is 2x (100 ms vs 50 ms). Against the strong tiled baseline it is 30/50 = 0.6x. The baseline choice flips the conclusion.

recall.question: Name three common baseline cheats.
recall.answer: Untuned baseline hyperparameters, a smaller baseline budget, and an easier baseline task.

keyTerms.definition: T^2 scores materialized with full activations stored.
Tiled attention, checkpointing, and cache reuse.

recall.question: What does the unit chapter plate show?
recall.answer: Three regions: naive cost, the stored objects (weights, KV cache, activations), and managed cost. The bottom line: memory buys parallelism, bandwidth bills every token.

sections.title: Russian-doll ladder: the autoregressive decode step (major mechanism)

keyTerms.definition: One generated token: its cost and what would change the answer.
Append new K/V and read all cached pairs.

recall.question: What is the Shell 5 invariant of the decode ladder?
recall.answer: The cache grows by 2Ln numbers per step, and rows of attention sum to 1.

recall.question: What breaks if you remove the causal mask (Shell 7)?
recall.answer: The model peeks at the future and generation quality collapses.

keyTerms.definition: Training costs 6P FLOPs per token; the research engineer's profiling number.
The formula that sizes every LLM deployment.
Versus task accuracy: the honesty check on every quality claim.

recall.question: What two numbers does a research engineer carry into any profiling session?
recall.answer: The 6P rule and the crossover T = 6n.
